messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For twenty-two years, Raymond had driven the same route through the city, his hands steady on the wheel, his eyes scanning the familiar streets. At sixty-one, he knew every pothole, every traffic light, and every regular passenger by face if not by name. But that was before the night six months ago when he had pulled into the depot after the last run and found three men waiting for him in the empty lot. They had been passengers earlier that week, he realized later—men who had ridden his bus for several days, watching, learning his schedule. They had cornered him between the bus and the chain-link fence, and for what felt like hours but was probably less than forty minutes, they had beaten him with tire irons and a length of pipe, demanding money he did not have, threatening his wife, his children, his home. Raymond had done nothing. He had not fought back, had not run, had not even shouted for help. He had simply curled on the asphalt and taken it, and the memory of his own stillness during those minutes was now more unbearable than the fractures and contusions that had healed.

What haunted Raymond most was not the pain but the gaps. He could see the first man’s boots approaching, the glint of the pipe under the depot’s flickering light, the taste of blood and gravel in his mouth. But between those images there was nothing—blank spaces, missing time, whole minutes that had simply vanished. And yet the terror had not vanished. Every time he tried to piece together what had happened, the same suffocating fear rose in his chest, as immediate and complete as if he were still lying on that asphalt. He would find himself shaking, his palms slick with sweat, his heart hammering so hard he thought he might pass out. His wife, Linda, would find him standing in the kitchen at two in the morning, listening. He told her he could not sleep, but the truth was that he could not stop listening—for footsteps on the porch, for the creak of a floorboard, for the sound of someone trying the front door. During the day, he could almost convince himself he was safe. But as soon as dusk settled, a deep, animal vigilance took over. He checked the locks three times before bed, then again at midnight, then again at three. He had taken to sleeping on the couch in the living room, where he could see both the front and back doors, where he could hear the street.

The worst part, Raymond believed, was that he had failed. He had failed to protect himself, and more than that, he had failed to protect Linda. What if they had come inside the house? What if they had hurt her while he lay there doing nothing? He had replayed that night a thousand times, each time imagining himself grabbing the tire iron, fighting back, saving them both. But he had not, and he was certain now that this revealed something fundamental about who he was. He was weak. A real man would have done something. A real man would not have let himself be beaten on the ground like a dog. Raymond could not forgive himself for his inaction, and the shame had settled into his bones like a low-grade fever that never broke.

At work, the triggers were everywhere. Every time a passenger stepped onto the bus with a hood pulled low, Raymond’s hands would tighten on the wheel and his chest would constrict. He had started driving with his eyes constantly flicking to the rearview mirror, scanning the faces behind him for anyone who looked wrong, anyone who might be watching him the way those three had watched him. He had begun to dread the evening shift, the long dark streets, the empty stops. Twice he had called in sick rather than drive the night route, and his supervisor had warned him that his attendance was becoming a problem. Linda had started sleeping in the guest room because his restlessness kept her awake, and she had asked him, gently, if he thought he might need to talk to someone. He had snapped at her, then apologized, then lain awake on the couch for the rest of the night, listening to the silence and waiting for the sound of boots on the porch.

It was Linda who finally made the appointment. She had found him in the bathroom at three in the morning, standing in the dark with his ear pressed to the door, and she had told him, not unkindly, that this could not go on. Raymond had agreed because he was exhausted, because he could not remember the last time he had felt safe, because he was afraid that if he did not get help, the next time someone came for him, he really would be too weak to do anything. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, listening to the hum of the fluorescent lights, and he thought about how strange it was to be afraid of silence now, when all he had ever wanted was for the noise to stop.
